questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why export dependency survived the end of colonial rule
questions.stem: A dispatch card on the board asks why customs revenue in a newly independent state still tracked the old colonial shipping calendar two decades after independence.

options.text: The port authority kept colonial tariffs because no new freight contracts had been signed.
options.misconception: assumes old tariffs were legally compulsory

options.text: Nations signed treaties obliging them to keep shipping ties, so revenue could not change.
options.misconception: believes colonial trade rules were binding treaties

options.text: Export earnings still came from a few colonial-era commodities sold abroad, so income followed foreign demand.
Inland roads were never built, so collected taxes could not reach the central treasury.
options.misconception: blames domestic transport for export dependence

questions.explanation: Independence changed sovereignty, not the structure of the economy. Exports were still raw commodities sold in old imperial markets, so national income tracked foreign prices rather than domestic policy.
questions.hint: Ask what the country sold and who bought it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Emergency rule as a method of control
questions.learningObjective: Explain the rationale military officers gave for suspending civilian rule
questions.stem: Beside the emergency-decree file, a supervisor asks why officers who had sworn to respect civilian rule came to suspend it themselves.

options.text: Because rival parties kept deadlocking, so officers saw a takeover as the only way to keep running.
options.misconception: treats deadlock alone as warrant for seizing power

options.text: Because civilian institutions were seen as too weak, so emergency rule was offered as a way to hold the country together.
Because the officers had been trained abroad to seize power whenever a government refused to govern.
options.misconception: invents foreign training as the real cause

options.text: Because voters had awarded the officers control of the state in a free and fair election.
options.misconception: claims the takeover followed a legitimate election win

questions.explanation: Officers argued civilian institutions were too weak to manage crisis, so emergency rule was sold as order-preserving. No election transferred power to them, so the reasoning was political, not electoral.
questions.hint: Ask what the regime said about civilian institutions.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Draw only the conclusions that a comparison table supports
questions.stem: The comparison sheet on the board lists two territories: the first won independence after three years of guerrilla war and 4,200 recorded combat deaths, the second after two years of constitutional talks with no organised armed revolt.

options.text: The second territory's talks produced stronger civilian institutions than the first territory's war did.
options.misconception: reads political quality into cost figures alone

options.text: The two territories should be judged identical because independence in both cases ended colonial rule.
options.misconception: treats the shared outcome as erasing real differences

options.text: Both routes to independence depended mainly on metropolitan politics rather than local pressure.
options.misconception: assumes distant pressure outweighed local action

options.text: The first paid a much higher human cost, but the sheet cannot show which path produced steadier governments.

questions.explanation: The sheet records time, cost and method only. Nothing in it measures later stability, so any claim about which route produced better governments goes beyond the evidence shown.
questions.hint: Only judge what the columns actually measure.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a young federation came apart over the distribution of authority
questions.stem: Pinned above the route map, a note asks why a federation that had existed for only a decade broke apart along a line drawn by language and region.

answer.exemplar: The breakup came from how the federation had been built. The central government in the capital controlled most spending and posts, while the distant region supplied troops, raw materials and food. When the centre tried to impose a constitution and a budget that the other region read as a threat to its own identity, its leaders declared independence, and the central state answered with force. Years of war and famine followed before the smaller territory was recognised, showing that a young union held together by force rather than consent can come apart quickly.

questions.explanation: Coercive unions split when the centre imposes decisions on a major region. Local leaders then call separation a defence of their interests, and the war that follows is about authority, not borders.
questions.hint: Link the political dispute to the use of force.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify planning signals in a colonial administrative memorandum

stimulus.body: A colonial office memorandum of 1954 instructs the regional administrator to prepare constitutional proposals that will vest full legislative authority in an elected local assembly. It further requires that a schedule of transfers for each administrative function be published within the year.

questions.stem: Scrawled on the board's edge, a note asks what the memorandum reveals about how the colonial power intended to end its rule.

options.text: The transfer was planned as a staged move to local control, with a timetable set in advance by the departing power.
The administrators had already decided to abandon their duties without any handover arrangements at all.
options.misconception: assumes the plan existed only to exit quickly

options.text: The timetable was a temporary measure meant to postpone full independence indefinitely.
options.misconception: reads the fixed deadline as indefinite delay

options.text: Local assemblies were intended as advisory bodies with no legislative power of their own.
options.misconception: assumes the assembly role was merely advisory

questions.explanation: A published timetable and instructions to draft a local assembly show planning, not improvisation. Self-government is treated as a scheduled transfer of legal authority, which is what a planned transition looks like.
questions.hint: Look for the timeline in the wording.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Combine imperial strain and local mobilisation in explaining decolonisation
questions.stem: Two timetables pinned side by side on the board set independence dates for territories whose metropolitan economies were all under strain in the same year, and the note asks what that pattern shows.

options.text: Economic weakness in the metropolitan country was the sole cause of every independence movement.
options.misconception: treats one factor as the single universal cause

options.text: Economic strain raised the cost of empire, while local movements supplied the pressure that turned retreat into independence.
Local mass support had no bearing, because colonial states surrendered whenever their finances ran short.
options.misconception: denies local agency in the transfer of power

options.text: The overlap shows timing was random, since strain and mobilisation occurred at unrelated moments.
options.misconception: reads coincidence as evidence of no connection

questions.explanation: One cause is not enough. Imperial financial strain made rule expensive, but local organisation decided whether that pressure produced negotiation or armed struggle, and on what terms.
questions.hint: Two causes can work at once.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why independence and state authority were proclaimed together
questions.stem: Alongside the depot notice, a commentary asks why two architects of an Asian declaration insisted that independence and the holding of state authority were proclaimed in the same breath.

options.text: They wanted to reassure foreign traders that business could continue under a stable new government.
options.misconception: reduces the proclamation to commercial reassurance

options.text: They needed to warn neighbouring states that the new state would defend its borders by force.
options.misconception: reads a threat of military force into the text

options.text: They wanted to be certain that the declaration was reported accurately in the foreign press.
options.misconception: focuses on press coverage rather than sovereignty

options.text: They wanted the declaration to count as a transfer of sovereignty, not merely a statement of hope.

questions.explanation: Proclaiming the state and its authority together made the act a claim to rule, which recognition later turned on. A mere statement of hope could be dismissed as opinion, with no government behind the claim.

questions.learningObjective: Describe the constitutional steps by which a colony became independent
questions.stem: Posted at the depot gate, a notice describes how a west African territory built an elected assembly in 1956 and then handed over authority the following year.

options.text: A military government dissolved the assembly and declared independence by decree alone.
options.misconception: recalls a coup instead of an elected transfer

options.text: The colonial power withdrew after losing a war fought inside the territory's own borders.
options.misconception: mistakes a negotiated transfer for a defeated one

options.text: Elected representatives took their seats and the colonial constitution was replaced by a domestic one.
A constituent assembly voted to join a federation that already had its own working government.
options.misconception: confuses joining a federation with becoming independent

questions.explanation: Ghana's path ran through elections, an enlarging assembly and a new constitution, then a negotiated handover of authority. No coup or internal war of conquest appears in that sequence.
questions.hint: Check which steps involved an election.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read what falling export shares do and do not show
questions.stem: A ledger card in the board shows export shares over time: raw cocoa and cotton made up 78 percent of export earnings in 1960, 71 percent in 1970 and 64 percent in 1980, with manufactures rising slowly over the same two decades.

options.text: By 1980 the economy had fully industrialised and no longer depended on raw commodities at all.
options.misconception: reads a declining share as complete diversification

options.text: Raw commodity exports still dominated earnings in 1980, so export dependence had eased rather than ended.
The falling share proves the country had stopped trading with its former colonial power.
options.misconception: assumes old buyers were abandoned entirely

options.text: The data shows that earnings rose every year even though the commodity share of them fell.
options.misconception: infers rising income from a falling percentage

questions.explanation: The share fell from 78 to 64 percent, but most earnings still came from raw materials in 1980. That is partial diversification at most; the card says nothing about partners or total income.
questions.hint: Read the final column before concluding.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Emergency rule as a method of control
questions.learningObjective: Trace the steps by which emergency rule became a permanent method of control
questions.stem: Under the depot clock, a note asks for an account of how emergency rule was used as a method of control in a newly independent state, naming who exercised the power and what argument justified it.

answer.exemplar: Emergency rule was used to concentrate decision-making in the hands of officers who claimed that elected institutions could not manage the country's problems. Having seized or inherited power, they suspended the constitution, closed legislatures and courts, and governed through decrees. The justification was that civilian institutions had proved too weak, too corrupt or too slow to handle a crisis, so a temporary emergency would restore order before power was handed back. In practice the emergency was never ended, because ending it would surrender the very authority that justified seizing it.

questions.explanation: The question asks for a reasoned account, not a list, so a strong answer links emergency powers to the political goal of control. It should also note that the promised return to civilian rule rarely arrived.
questions.hint: Link the legal tool to the political purpose.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Infer bargaining strength from the record of a negotiation

stimulus.body: Minutes of a conference held in the metropolitan capital record that the government offered self-government within a year. The local delegates are described as demanding a date certain for independence, and the meeting closed without agreement on the timetable.

questions.stem: The torn corner of a memo asks what the minutes reveal about the balance of strength between metropolitan negotiators and local delegates.

options.text: The metropolitan government controlled the outcome, since only its delegates could make binding commitments.
options.misconception: assumes colonial delegations alone could bind the future

options.text: The delegates had no bargaining position, because the minutes record no agreement at all.
options.misconception: treats the absence of agreement as proof of no leverage

options.text: The conference shows local delegates could dictate terms, because their demands went unchallenged.
options.misconception: mistakes recorded demands for accepted terms

options.text: Each side needed the other, since a date certain was refused and no agreement could be reached alone.

questions.explanation: The metropolitan side could offer but not impose a timetable, and the local side could demand but not guarantee it. No agreement is evidence of mutual dependence rather than weakness on either side.
questions.hint: Neither side could proceed without the other.

questions.learningObjective: Combine political and fiscal causes of a federation's collapse
questions.stem: Filed beside the rolling stock diagram, two cards attribute a federation's collapse, one to a contested constitution and the other to a sudden fall in the central government's income.

options.text: The constitution alone caused the split, since every dispute in the union began with its text.
options.misconception: makes one document the sole explanation

options.text: The revenue collapse alone caused the split, since financial stress always precedes political rupture.
options.misconception: generalises from a single case to a rule

options.text: The revenue loss weakened the centre, while the constitutional dispute gave regional leaders the argument to act.
Neither factor mattered, since the split was the result of a decision taken entirely outside the country.
options.misconception: invokes an unexplained external cause

questions.explanation: Hold both cards at once: the political dispute supplied a justification for separation, and the fiscal shock made it hard for the centre to impose a settlement. Neither card alone explains the timing.
questions.hint: Two cards can describe one process.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why preparatory steps reveal a planned handover
questions.stem: Marked in blue pencil on the board, a checklist tracks the drafting of a constitution, the training of civil servants and the date set for the handover of authority.

options.text: The checklist shows that the transition was improvised once the decision to leave had already been taken.
options.misconception: reads planning as improvisation after the fact

options.text: The checklist shows that institutions and successors were prepared in advance of the handover date.
The checklist shows that local administrators were excluded from preparing for self-government.

options.text: The checklist shows that the transfer depended on the personal loyalty of one senior officer.
options.misconception: reduces institutional planning to one individual

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Select evidence that could genuinely test an economic explanation
questions.stem: Turned down at the depot office, a memo proposes an economic explanation for decolonisation and asks which evidence would best test it.

options.text: A study of how metropolitan governments allocated defence spending across their colonies.
options.misconception: ignores the spending that the explanation predicts

options.text: An account of the independence ceremonies and the flags chosen by the new governments.
options.misconception: mistakes symbolic detail for causal evidence

options.text: A history of the diplomatic language used at independence negotiations in each territory.
options.misconception: reads diplomatic wording as economic cause

options.text: A comparison of colonial trade earnings in the last decade of rule across several territories.

questions.explanation: An economic explanation predicts a pattern in trade and fiscal conditions, so a cross-territory comparison could confirm or weaken it. Ceremonial detail describes outcomes, not causes.
questions.hint: Choose evidence that varies with the proposed cause.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a calendar of dates from a declaration to a settlement
questions.stem: The depot wall carries a calendar of four dates: a Japanese surrender in mid-August 1945, a declaration of independence later that month, a British arrival in September, and a Dutch transfer of sovereignty at the end of the decade.

options.text: The declaration preceded the transfer of power by more than four years, so the claim was made long before it was recognised.
British arrival in September shows the declaration was made under British authority and therefore invalid.
options.misconception: treats later recognition as the basis of the original act

options.text: The four-year gap shows the declaration was forgotten and had to be revived by the transfer.
options.misconception: infers neglect from a long negotiating period

options.text: Because the dates run in order, the declaration was a legal consequence of the earlier surrender.
options.misconception: assumes sequence implies legal dependence

questions.explanation: The calendar separates the act of proclaiming independence from the recognition that followed it. A four-year interval shows a claim asserted early and settled later, not that the later settlement created the earlier claim.
questions.hint: Read the interval between the two ends.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an organised movement converted into the governing party of a new state
questions.stem: Noticed by the dispatcher, a card asks for an explanation of how an elected trade union movement turned into the governing party of an independent west African state.

answer.exemplar: The movement grew out of organised labour and anti-colonial pamphlets, and it turned that organisation into electoral support by presenting a programme of self-government, land reform and economic development rather than a call to leave the empire. Its leader pressed the colonial government to restore the legislative assembly that had been suspended, then won a decisive election and used the resulting majority to carry a constitution granting independence and a seat at the United Nations. The key point is that the change came through elections and constitutional negotiation rather than armed revolt.

questions.explanation: A strong answer traces organisation to electoral majority to constitutional change, making elections rather than revolt the decisive mechanism. The proposed programme of change matters as much as the tactics.
questions.hint: Trace the steps from organisation to the first budget.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read a financial memorandum as evidence of external exposure

stimulus.body: A finance ministry memorandum of 1966 observes that four commodities accounted for 82 percent of export earnings. It notes that the reserve fund held only five months of import cover and recommends negotiating long-term contracts with overseas buyers.

options.text: The country had already achieved a diversified industrial base and needed only better marketing abroad.
options.misconception: assumes diversification is stated in the memo

options.text: Dependence on a few commodity exports and thin reserves left the country exposed to outside markets.
The government intended to end exports of primary commodities well within the coming decade.
options.misconception: misreads a recommendation as a policy of abandonment

options.text: Shortages of foreign exchange were caused by a deliberate refusal to earn revenue abroad.
options.misconception: blames policy intent for a structural problem

questions.explanation: Concentration in four commodities plus thin reserves marks an economy exposed to price swings abroad. The recommended long contracts confirm the government saw exposure as a problem to manage, not solved.
questions.hint: Note the concentration figures and the reserve cover.

options.misconception: narrows emergency rule to a single measure

options.text: The list of powers shows the emergency was legally narrow and therefore harmless in practice.
options.misconception: judges severity from legal form alone

options.text: The elections that followed prove the emergency government genuinely intended to hand power back.
options.misconception: takes one election as proof of lasting intent

options.text: The suspension of many powers combined with later elections shows control tightened first and was only partly reversed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what determined whether decolonisation was negotiated or fought
questions.stem: Circulated among depot staff, a memo asks why some territories left empire through negotiation while others had to be fought free, and what the difference turned on.

options.text: The deciding factor was simply the size of each territory, with larger colonies always fighting.
options.misconception: reduces the outcome to territorial size alone

options.text: The difference turned on how much organised local pressure was already in place when talks began.
The deciding factor was foreign rivalry, with metropolitan states fighting whenever rivals backed rebels.
options.misconception: makes outside rivalry the constant explanation

options.text: The deciding factor was colonial race policy, since harsher rule always provoked armed resistance.
options.misconception: assumes harsher rule always provokes revolt

questions.explanation: Talks moved fastest where local organisations existed to make refusal costly; armed struggle broke out where such pressure was thin. Size and foreign rivalry mattered, but through local organisation.
questions.hint: Ask what the refusing side faced in each case.

questions.learningObjective: Identify structural causes named in a letter about a federation's collapse

options.text: The letter blames a single foreign power for the collapse of the union and its institutions.

questions.learningObjective: Read a handover schedule as evidence of a staged transition
questions.stem: The fare table lists a transition schedule: a constitution drafted in year one, a legislative assembly elected in year two, ministers appointed in year three and full authority transferred in year four.

The schedule shows the transfer was a single event that was simply delayed until the fourth year.
options.misconception: collapses a staged sequence into one moment

options.misconception: reads a published date as a broken promise

options.text: The schedule shows that elected institutions were meant to take over at once in the very first year.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Describe a method for testing competing explanations of decolonisation
questions.stem: Written on the back of a duty roster, a note asks for an account of how a historian might test competing explanations of why decolonisation happened when it did.

answer.exemplar: Testing means specifying what each explanation predicts and then looking for evidence that would count against it. An economic account predicts that territories with collapsing metropolitan trade or rising defence costs would move first, so trade and budget series for several empires can be compared against the dates of independence. A nationalist account predicts that mass mobilisation preceded transfers, so party membership, petition volumes and strike dates should lead the transfer date. A good test uses cases where one explanation fits and another does not, and states in advance what result would count as disproof.

questions.explanation: The note asks for a method, so the answer must define predictions, evidence and the possibility of disproof rather than list causes. It should also use several territories to avoid resting on one case.
questions.hint: State what each explanation predicts first.

options.misconception: narrows the claim to a single island group

options.text: The announcement addressed officials directly, treating the claim as an order to be obeyed at once.

questions.explanation: Addressing officials assumes a state apparatus that has already changed hands, which is a claim to rule rather than to negotiate. Requests for aid or references to acceptance would point the other way.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a federation declared permanent in its founding failed within a decade
questions.stem: Left on the dispatch desk, a sheet asks for an explanation of why a federation dissolved within a decade of its creation despite having been declared permanent at its founding.

answer.exemplar: The founding declaration treated permanence as a guarantee, but permanence had been asserted rather than built. The central constitution concentrated law-making, currency and the appointment of officials in the capital, while the constituent regions supplied most of the land, the taxes and the recruits. Because the regions were represented through a chamber with no power over the budget, every effort to divide resources produced a new dispute. When the central leadership pushed a constitution that the eastern region read as a settlement against its interests, that region's leaders declared independence and mobilised their own administration and army. The central state, unwilling to concede, fought a long war whose costs ended the federation's institutions along with its territory.

questions.explanation: The sheet asks why proclaimed permanence failed, so the answer must trace the gap between declarations and the real division of power and resources. Naming the constitutional dispute is the heart of it.
questions.hint: Contrast the promise with how power was shared.

questions.explanation: Training existing staff and publishing a schedule of transfers are both preparation for a managed handover. Secrecy would defeat a published schedule, and the document concerns functions rather than declarations.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Emergency rule as a method of control
questions.learningObjective: Trace how an emergency regime extended control and made it permanent
questions.stem: Rejected at the depot office, a request asks for an account of the steps by which an emergency regime secured control of a state and then extended that control over time.

answer.exemplar: The sequence typically began with a crisis that the civilian government was said to be unable to manage, sometimes used as the pretext for action. Officers then issued decrees that suspended or overrode the constitution, closed the legislature and courts, and placed key ministries, borders and the security services under their own control. Opposition parties were banned or their leaders detained, and a new constitution was announced to give the arrangement a legal appearance. The last step was the most revealing: the emergency was extended or the promised handover deferred, so a temporary instrument became a permanent system, and the absence of elections left the regime unaccountable.

questions.explanation: The request asks for a sequence, so the answer should move from the stated crisis through legal suspension to the extension of control, and end by explaining why the emergency was never allowed to expire.
questions.hint: End with why the emergency was never wound down.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a territory achieved self-government in little over a decade
questions.stem: Called out during a depot meeting, a question asks for an explanation of how a territory that had been governed for generations achieved self-government in little over a decade.

answer.exemplar: The short timetable was the result of several developments arriving together. A mass movement organised outside the colonial institutions gave ordinary people a reason to expect change, and its leaders gave the demand a programme rather than a grievance list. Those leaders pressed for the return of the legislative assembly that the colonial government had suspended, which forced the issue onto the metropolitan agenda at a moment when the authority was less willing and less able to resist. An election then produced a large majority for the movement, and the metropolitan government concluded that a transfer on terms was safer than a long confrontation. Constitutional drafting and a negotiated handover completed the process, giving the new state a parliament, a civil service and international recognition.

questions.explanation: The question asks for an explanation of speed, so the answer must combine organisation, electoral leverage and metropolitan constraint rather than credit one alone. Naming the sequence of steps is what makes it an explanation.
questions.hint: Combine organisation, elections and metropolitan constraint.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Set out how a historian could test a claim about imperial weakness
questions.stem: Paired on the board with a map, a question asks for an account of how a historian might use evidence from several territories to test the claim that decolonisation was caused by the weakness of imperial economies.

answer.exemplar: The test begins by making the claim precise, because a general reference to imperial weakness can be supported by almost any date. The historian should specify what weakness means, for example falling customs revenue, rising defence costs or difficulty borrowing, and state what the claim predicts for each territory. If weakness drove transfers, territories whose empires were weakest should have moved first, once local pressure is held constant. The historian then gathers comparable fiscal series for the same years, checks that local mobilisation did not simply run ahead of them, and looks for cases where a strong imperial economy still produced an early transfer. Any such case weakens the claim, while consistent ordering strengthens it.

questions.explanation: The question asks for a method, so the answer must state what the claim predicts, gather comparable evidence across territories, and consider cases that could weaken it. Declaring the claim plausible is not a test.
questions.hint: Make the claim precise before gathering evidence.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how members who never governed together reached separation
questions.stem: Timed against the board's schedule, a question asks for an account of how a federation whose founding members had never governed together ended up dividing into two states.

answer.exemplar: The members had been joined by a treaty that promised a shared future without ever agreeing how power would be divided. The constitution that followed put law-making, the currency and the appointment of officials in the capital, and gave the outlying member a legislature with no power over the budget. That arrangement survived only while resources were plentiful. When costs rose and money had to be apportioned, every negotiation over shares reopened the question of who was a member and who was a subject. The outlying member's leaders argued that majority rule was being used to settle a question of consent, and they began to prepare their own institutions. The central government read those preparations as a threat and moved first with its armed forces, which converted a political disagreement into a war. Years of fighting and economic ruin followed, and the union's central institutions did not survive the war at all.

questions.explanation: The answer must follow the constitution, the resource dispute and the escalation to war. The shift from political dispute to armed conflict needs explicit mention, not just a list of grievances.
questions.hint: Follow the path from constitution to resource dispute to war.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Draw a conclusion about fiscal strain from lists of negotiated and fought transfers
questions.stem: Tested by the board's working group, two lists are compared: territories that transferred after organised negotiation, and territories that transferred after armed struggle, with the metropolitan fiscal condition noted for each.

options.text: The two lists show that organised negotiation was chosen only where imperial finances were healthy.
options.misconception: claims a pattern the notes do not show

options.text: The two lists show that armed struggle always followed a complete collapse in imperial finances.
options.misconception: asserts an absolute rule about fiscal collapse

options.text: The lists suggest both routes operated under varied fiscal conditions, so fiscal strain cannot alone pick the route.
The two lists show that fiscal conditions were irrelevant, since the notes record nothing else at all.
options.misconception: dismisses the notes without reading them

questions.explanation: If the same fiscal condition appears on both lists, fiscal strain cannot be the variable that chose the route. That narrows the explanation without deciding it, since other differences remain to be examined.
questions.hint: Look for shared conditions across the two lists.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a declaration preceded the machinery of government
questions.stem: Taped beside the board's timetables, a note asks why the authors of a 1945 declaration insisted on announcing the state's existence before any administrative machinery existed.

options.text: Because the declaration was required to make the territory eligible for membership of the United Nations.
options.misconception: invents a constitutional requirement the note does not state

options.text: Because asserting the claim first established a government to negotiate from, rather than one to receive.
Because the declaration gave the new government time to build an administration before the handover.
options.misconception: reads the declaration as a device for buying time

options.text: Because the colonial authorities had already announced their own intention to withdraw.
options.misconception: assumes advance notice by the colonial power

questions.explanation: Order matters. A claim proclaimed while the administration is still in colonial hands creates a government that negotiates with the departing power, rather than a subordinate office that only receives orders.
questions.hint: Ask who would be at the table afterwards.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read institutional growth alongside a growing electoral mandate
questions.stem: Read from the board's daily sheet, a column compares a colony with its future self: assembly members elected, sitting days granted, ministries created, and years from election to independence.

options.text: The figures show that more elected members meant a shorter wait for self-government.
options.misconception: assumes a numeric link the column cannot support

options.text: The figures show that independence came soonest where the assembly sat least often.
options.misconception: invents an inverse rule about sitting days

options.text: The figures show that the number of ministries created decided how many years the wait took.
options.misconception: picks one column and treats it as decisive

options.text: The figures show gradual institutional growth alongside a growing elected mandate over the same years.

questions.explanation: Members elected, sitting days and ministries all rise while the wait continues, which is what the build-up of self-government looks like from inside. The column shows co-movement, not which factor caused the outcome.
questions.hint: Look at how the columns move together.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an inherited economy kept export dependence for decades
questions.stem: Filed in the depot's revenue folder, a question asks for an account of how an economy inherited from colonial rule continued to depend on a narrow range of exports for decades after independence.

answer.exemplar: The dependence lasted because everything around it had been built for it. The railways ran to the mines and plantations rather than between regional capitals, the port sheds were built for one commodity, the schools trained clerks for a colonial export department, and the revenue system taxed exports because that was where the money was. When the new state took over, these arrangements produced an immediate loss of revenue if changed and no gain if kept, so they were kept. Foreign buyers then gained leverage over prices and over the exchange value of the currency, while governments that needed revenue for other purposes found the export sector the only reliable source. Over time a manufacturing sector began to appear, but it grew beside the old structures rather than replacing them, and the share of earnings from raw commodities declined only slowly. The result was an economy where national income tracked world commodity prices and where the state could not easily change course.

questions.explanation: The account must explain why inherited structures kept producing dependence, not merely list them. Linking infrastructure, revenue and foreign bargaining power, then noting the slow pace of change, answers the question.
questions.hint: Explain why the inherited arrangements were kept.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Emergency rule as a method of control
questions.learningObjective: Read a decree as evidence of concentrated power

stimulus.body: A decree of 1966 announces that the constitution is suspended and that the legislature will not meet. It states that political parties will not be permitted to operate and that a commission of senior officers will exercise all legislative authority until further notice.

questions.stem: Held against the board's calendar, a decree asks what the document shows about the concentration of power.

options.text: The decree shows that the officers intended to restore the legislature once calm had returned.
options.misconception: reads an open-ended suspension as a temporary measure

options.text: The decree concentrates law-making in a small body while removing the legislature and the parties.
The decree shows that political parties had agreed to suspend their activities voluntarily.
options.misconception: invents consent where the decree commands

options.text: The decree shows that the officers had been elected to their positions by the legislature.
options.misconception: claims an electoral origin for an appointed body

questions.explanation: Suspending the legislature and the parties, while giving law-making power to senior officers, is a description of concentrated control. The text suggests no voluntary agreement, electoral origin or fixed end date.
questions.hint: Add up what the decree suspends and who rules.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how local organisation and metropolitan strain can operate together
questions.stem: Set beside the board with a map of routes, two accounts of a territory's departure from empire are set side by side: one emphasises local organisation, the other the state of metropolitan finances.

options.text: The two accounts are rivals, and the map of routes shows which one the evidence supports.
options.misconception: treats a map of routes as settling a causal dispute

options.text: The two accounts are rivals, so one of them must be wrong in the end.
options.misconception: assumes explanatory factors must compete

options.text: The two accounts describe conditions that can reinforce each other rather than compete.
The two accounts are irrelevant, since the map of routes shows only where goods were moved.
options.misconception: dismisses the accounts because of an unrelated map

questions.explanation: Local organisation and metropolitan strain are different kinds of condition: one supplies pressure, the other supplies cost and opportunity. They can reinforce each other, so need not be scored as rivals.
questions.hint: Ask whether both conditions can operate at once.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a federation that held together from one that fractured
questions.stem: Checked against the board's timetable, a case asks which factor best distinguishes a federation that broke apart from one that held together after independence.

options.text: Whether the regions shared institutions capable of settling disputes about power without war.
Whether the federation had been given a long time to develop before independence arrived.
options.misconception: picks an irrelevant factor about length of time

options.text: Whether the leader of the central government had been in office for a long period.
options.misconception: reduces the outcome to one officeholder's tenure

options.text: Whether the federation had a larger territory than the states around it at the time.
options.misconception: invites a size comparison that explains little

questions.explanation: Federations that hold together settle disputes over the distribution of power without arms. Missing that, a quarrel about authority becomes a question of who can compel, and the union fractures.
questions.hint: Ask how a quarrel about power could be settled.
